The University of Colorado presents discussions of major issues of our time.
featuring members of the faculty and student body of the university and outstanding visitors to the
campus at Boulder. Are there really flying saucers? Are they from Earth or from other planets? Are they
flown by creatures from somewhere in space? These are some of the questions which people everywhere
horror asking. Some say anything seems possible in our space age. Others say completely ridiculous.
In any case, the issue, one of the hottest potatoes in the world of research,
has been tossed to the University of Colorado.
The Air Force, which has collected and investigated many thousands of reports of such
unidentified flying objects, has asked the Colorado Institution to evaluate these reports
and to make a general investigation of the sightings which have become probably the biggest mystery of our time.
Chosen to lead the investigation at Colorado is one of the outstanding scientists of today, Dr. Edward U. Condon,
now a professor of physics at CU, formerly director of the National Bureau of Standards,
a scientific advisor to the Special Senate Committee on Atomic Energy, and president of the American Physical Society.
I'm trying to find that we have an interesting opportunity to study a lot of those peculiar reports, peculiar observations.
A great deal of these things have perfectly ordinary and commonplace explanations,
but there's a little overdue of maybe about 5% that are most difficult to explain, and we're going to try to fuggle it out.
Do you have any qualms about being able to make this a scientific inquiry?
Well, I think we can make it a scientific inquiry, all right, but how far we'll get in finding clear and critically tested answers to the important questions is another matter.
Could you tell me how the University of Colorado was chosen for this job?
Well, I don't know in the sense of to what extent other places were considered.
I think this is a natural place in view of the intimate relationship that we have here
with the National Center for Atmospheric Research and the radio propagation laboratories of the government,
which are now the Environmental Science Services Administration.
and then it happens that our work here in physics is rather strongly oriented towards astrophysics and atmospheric phenomena.
What is the specific assignment from the airport?
Well, they just want us to, the formal title of the project is Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects,
and they want us to examine and to report and to do additional field work and experimental work
and whatever in our judgment contributes most to understanding it.
That is, we don't have any assignment in the sense of them telling us how to operate.
But we do have considerable freedom at the university.
We have absolute, complete freedom to do whatever we like, whatever we think is best on this,
have absolute and complete freedom to publish our findings without to acquire clearance
from the airport.
Do you expect to be collecting any new data through your office?
Yes, but we prefer to have the material from all sources reported directly to the
nearest airport base in the country.
I should say also that, strictly on grounds of keeping the job within practical limits,
we don't expect to look into cases reported from other countries.
Not that we wouldn't be interested in them, but we can't...
It would just be impractical from a travel point of view and things of that sort.
There are probably thousands of people who have seen flying objects
them who haven't reported these sightings to the airport. Now, would you suggest that
these people contact your office?
Well, in general, we prefer that the, that either individuals in the public or police
officers or others who know about these things should report, if possible, when possible,
to build to the nearest Air Force base.
I should add that the Air Force itself intends to strengthen its program
by having some of the officers to do a more thorough job of field investigation
than they have done in the past.
So they'll be strengthening their program at the same time that we are undertaking to do ours.
Since this project is assigned to the university by the Air Force,
I suppose that it must be assumed the Air Force's interest in this is not one of hiding facts, but of exposing the facts.
Yes, I think that's right. So far as I can tell so far, they want to make everything open and available.
Now, critics of the Air Force, who have passed the code behavior, have made some pretty strong accusations to the contrary,
but I don't believe that.
It's possible that in times past that maybe they were holding information back,
but I don't believe they are now or I don't believe they intend to in the future.
What so far would you say are the biggest problems that you see in this project?
Well, there are two that I'd like to take the opportunity to comment on.
One is the fact that well over 90% of the reports that come in
turn out to be perfectly ordinary phenomena,
and so it makes quite a burden on the investigators
to have to look into all those things to eliminate them.
On the other hand, the other problem is just to do it opposite of it,
namely that this subject has been the bed of so many jokes
I'm not so humiliated by being ridiculed for having admitted to having seen these things,
but I know that there are lots of people who have experiences of this sort who are reluctant to report them.
And we would hope to win their confidence and overcome their reluctance and get full cooperation that way.
So on the one hand, we'd like to get fewer reports by helping people to understand ordinary phenomena better,
so they wouldn't be confused by that.
and would like to get more reports from people who have been hesitant about reporting them.
I might say that we will, whenever requested, a person who might give us a report
and would rather not have his name made public in connection with it,
we will keep such reports confidential, let us say keep the name of the reporting person confidential.
Do you feel that as a scientist you have a natural skepticism towards reports of UFO sightings?
Well, I think everybody has to have a skepticism. Let's take the most extreme view, the notion that some of these things do represent things sent here from outer space from a different civilization.
Well, it's such an extraordinarily important or amazing thing, if it were true, that one
wants to subject the so-called evidence to the highest level of criticism before he begins
to believe it.
The more out of line and improbable a thing is, the more evidence you want to have before
you believe it.
I understand some of our scientists say that there are few reasons why we shouldn't expect life on other planets and other galaxies.
Yes, that part seems to be pretty well concluded, although it's very well speculated in nature.
But the feeling is that wherever conditions that would support life exist, the chances are life has a root as a reason.

On the other hand, all of these other places are so far away that it's extraordinarily difficult to suppose that those people are able to, if they exist, are able to actually travel here and come here by any means that we can picture.
What types of people will be involved?
Well, there are mostly physicists and astronomers and astrophysics and meteorologists.
Some work involving behavioral scientists, social scientists, one way or another.
Of course, it must be borne in mind that we won't have an enormous staff of people.
The funds available don't permit that, but there'll probably be quite a large number,
On the other side, there were over 100 people involved, considering that many of them would be part-time consultants.
For that matter, I myself am only going to do about half-time on it because I have other duties that I can't neglect.
It's for 15 months.
But strictly speaking, it won't start November 1st.
And it's to run until about, I don't know, whatever, 15 months.
I guess that's the first of February of 68.
How definite are the plans now for the university's participation in this?
Well, the fact that we're going to is pretty definite.
But the detail and specific thing, what we're doing now,
who hold the first of these conferences and meetings
and bringing in some outside consultants
who've had prior experience in this field
to make more specific plans.
I would assume that that phase of the matter
would take till about the 1st of next February,
giving us about a next year as to what afterwards makes sense.
I assume many people have seen things
without taking any great amount of detailed notes
or specific information, would you like to make any recommendations on how people should investigate?
Well, we will. We'll be wanting to do that after we've given a little more thought,
but I'm not really prepared to do that now. I think that's one of the important things.
We're thinking in terms of getting out a manual for observers,
a thing that could be widely distributed in schools and to police officers and so on,
so as to warn them about the things that might be overlooked
if they didn't have it drawn to their attention
so as to improve the quality of the reports that come in.
In conclusion, we asked Professor Condon,
what do you think about the sensational books and articles
we've been reading about flying saucers,
people who claim to have seen the creatures that fly them,
and even those who say that they've been aboard the strange space vehicle?
Well, no, I haven't read very many of them. I've read a few. Many of them have a rather
sensational approach, that is, they act just because they think they're first get you to
admit the possibility that people come from outer space, then they're first in the native
health ministry to establish it, which of course they haven't done. And then I guess
many of them are full of controversial elements of one sort or another and that just meant,
I think, that popular reading. They're not very scientific. But if you strip away that kind of
thing that is predominant in many of them, there is a kind of a central core of facts about specific
cases that's interesting. It gives a first guide to the kind of thing that will have to be studied.
So, it may be that a team of scientists looking into the reports of strange objects in the
sky will admit there are visitors from space watching us, or the University of Colorado
project may disprove any such conclusions.
Perhaps there will not be any definite answer possible.
In any case, the open-minded, careful investigators headed by Dr. Edward U. Condon are involved
in a fascinating search with the world waiting for their conclusion.
Our guest today, Dr. Edward U. Condon, Director of the Air Force Project Investigating Unidentified
Flying Objects at the University of Colorado.
This has been a special program in the series, Today's Challenge, discussing vital topics
of our time.
